1. What SutraFlow is

SutraFlow is a visual integration designer and engine. You build a Sutra by dragging activities from palettes onto a canvas and connecting them; you map data from earlier activities into later ones; you test and debug it in the studio; and you deploy it to run on the server: on a schedule, when a file or message arrives, or as a REST or SOAP API protected by a security policy and TLS.

One program contains three parts:

  • The studio at http://127.0.0.1:4800: the Designer, Runs, Resources and Server & APIs screens.
  • The engine, which runs Sutras step by step and saves each finished step, so runs survive a restart and long waits cost nothing.
  • The gateway on ports 8080 (HTTP) and 8443 (HTTPS), which serves deployed APIs, separately from the studio.
Words used in this guide

A project holds Sutras, shared resources (connections), schemas and variables. A Sutra is one process diagram. An activity is one box on it; a step is one execution of an activity in a run; a run is one execution of a Sutra. Sutra variables live for one run, Project variables are shared by a project's Sutras, and Sengine variables are server settings made by the administrator.

2. Install and start the server

SutraFlow needs Node.js 22.13 or later; version 24 is recommended. Nothing else is installed: the database is SQLite, built into Node.

Procedure

  1. Open a terminal in the SutraFlow folder.
  2. Install the packages: npm install
  3. Build the studio and server: npm run build
  4. Start the server: npm start
  5. Open http://127.0.0.1:4800. The first time, create the administrator account.

For development with automatic reload, run npm run dev and open http://localhost:5173. The tests run with npm test.

Guidelines

Back up the data folder, and above all data/master.key: without it the encrypted secrets cannot be read.
Keep the studio on 127.0.0.1. Publish APIs through the gateway ports, not the studio port.

Server settings

Environment variableDefaultMeaning
SUTRA_DATA_DIR./dataDatabase, master key, deployment config files.
SUTRA_MASTER_KEYthe key fileThe vault key, 32 bytes in base64.
SUTRA_ADMIN_HOST, SUTRA_ADMIN_PORT127.0.0.1, 4800Where the studio listens.
SUTRA_GATEWAY_HTTP_PORT, SUTRA_GATEWAY_HTTPS_PORT8080, 8443Gateway ports until changed in Server & APIs.
SUTRA_WORKERS16Steps that run at the same time.
SUTRA_MAX_STEPS10000Safety limit of steps per run.
SUTRA_REPLY_TIMEOUT_MS60000How long an API caller waits for the reply step.

3. The studio, screen by screen

The top bar holds the four screens, the version in the middle, the light/dark switch and Sign out.

ScreenWhat it is for
DesignerBuilding, testing, debugging and deploying Sutras. Left: the Project explorer and the Palettes. Middle: the canvas and its toolbar. Right: the selected activity's General, Input, Output and Settings tabs.
RunsEvery run with its status, steps, inputs and outputs, logs; approvals waiting for a person.
ResourcesShared connections and security of the current project, and the secrets vault.
Server & APIsExposed services, Sengine variables, gateway ports, TLS certificate, active listeners.

The Designer toolbar

  • Sutra list: opens another Sutra of the project.
  • + New Sutra: a blank Sutra or a starter (REST API, SOAP service, approval with timer).
  • ▶ Test: runs the current draft once with the trigger's test data, without deploying.
  • Debug: runs the draft one activity at a time (see Testing and debugging).
  • ↶ Undo and ↷ Redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z): step back and forward through your changes to the Sutra, up to 100 of them, such as a deleted activity or connection, a move or a changed mapping. While you type in a field, Ctrl+Z undoes the typing in that field instead.
  • Deploy: makes the current draft the live version.
  • Status badges: Saved, Deployed v2 or Draft only, and the last test result.

The Delete key deletes the selected activity or connection (Backspace does not, so editing text never removes an activity). Changes save automatically. Zoom with the wheel or the + and − buttons; the small map at the bottom left shows where you are.

4. Projects and the explorer

Open the Project tab on the left of the Designer. The project list at the top switches projects; + creates one. Each project holds:

SectionWhat it holds
SutrasThe Sutras, with their deployed version. Each Sutra also has Sutra variables, read as {vars.name}.
ResourcesThe project's connections and security, each listed under the name you gave it with a symbol for its kind. + opens the list of kinds: HTTP connection, Outbound security, API security policy, AI provider, Email (SMTP and IMAP), Database, Kafka, RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Firebase, OAuth connection. The name is its key in the deployment config, so you can rename it safely.
SchemasShared JSON (JSON Schema or a sample document) and XML (XSD) schemas. Activities pick them to describe payloads, bodies, CSV rows and mapping targets.
Service descriptorsWSDL files that Invoke SOAP service can call.
ConfigurationProject variables, the deployment config and the log file settings.

Add a connection

  1. Next to Resources, click + and choose the kind, for example HTTP connection.
  2. Give it your own name, such as Orders API. The explorer lists it under that name.
  3. Fill in its settings: address and port, user, the vault secret for the password. Settings marked {x} take a project variable, such as {{gv.ORDERS_URL}}, so each environment can use its own value.
  4. Click Test connection. SutraFlow tries the settings as they are on screen, with variables filled in, and says what happened: the HTTP status, the database it reached, the mailbox count, the AI model that answered.
  5. Click Save.

Add a shared schema

  1. Next to Schemas, click +.
  2. Give it a name and choose the type: JSON or XML (XSD).
  3. Paste the content, or load a file. A JSON sample document is enough; SutraFlow works out the fields.
  4. For an XSD with several root elements, choose the default root element.
  5. Save. The Fields tree shows the result: * marks a required field, ** a repeating one.

5. Building a Sutra

  1. Click + New Sutra and choose a starter, or start blank.
  2. Drag a trigger from the Triggers palette (or keep Manual start). A Sutra has one trigger.
  3. Drag activities onto the canvas. Search the palettes with the box at the top.
  4. Connect an activity's output (a circle on its right) to the next activity's input (on its left). Activities with several outputs, such as If / else or Router, have one circle per output.
  5. Select each activity and fill in its tabs.
  6. Click Test. Each activity shows its result; select one and open Output to see the values.
  7. When it works, click Deploy.

Branches, errors and ends

  • Every activity except triggers and End has a red error output. Connect it to handle a failure; otherwise the failure ends the run as failed.
  • A branch that is not taken is skipped; a Merge after it still continues.
  • End ends a branch. With Sutra: success or Sutra: error it stops the whole Sutra at once and cancels the other branches.
  • Throw error fails a branch with your message, so an error output before it can handle it.
  • The Error handler activity catches every error whose activity has no error output connected: one place to log, alert and clean up.

Connections: names and conditions

Click a connection to name it and decide when it is taken. The name and condition show on the canvas.

TakenMeaning
AlwaysEvery time the activity finishes on that output. The default.
When a condition is trueA formula on the previous activity's output, which it reads as {input.x}; for example ={input.amount} > 1000 named Order > 1000. Several "when" connections can be taken together.
OtherwiseTaken when none of the "when" connections from the same output was taken.

A connection that is not taken counts as a skipped branch, so a Merge after it still continues. For many routes, or for routes on the same message used in several places, a Router activity keeps them in one place.

Sample Sutras

Click + New Sutra, then Choose samples to tick the ones you want, or Add all. Test each one and open its activities' Input and Output tabs to see how it is built. Samples that write files use C:/sutra/samples; change the folder to suit your machine.

SampleWhat it showsPalettes

Reusable Sutras

Put logic used in several places in its own Sutra: a Manual start with a payload schema, the steps, and Return with the result. Other Sutras run it with Call Sutra, wait for the result and continue; a failure inside it arrives on Call Sutra's error output. While you test, the draft of the called Sutra runs; deployed Sutras call its deployed version.

Loops

Any activity can run more than once (Settings tab → Loop):

  • For each item of a list: once per item of Loop over. Map {iteration.value} (or {item}) and {iteration.index}; the mapper lists them under $iteration. The output is iterations (every result) and count.
  • Repeat while a condition holds: runs, then checks the condition, for example ={iteration.output.status} != 'DONE', with a delay between runs: polling until a job is finished. The output is the last result plus _iterations.

A looping activity shows ↻ after its type on the canvas. Each loop has a maximum number of runs (1000 by default).

Sutras working together

  • Call Sutra: run another Sutra and use its result.
  • Send to channel and Channel trigger: tell other deployed Sutras that something happened, in memory.
  • Counter: a number shared by all runs of the project, such as a sequence or a daily total.
Guidelines

Name activities by what they do (Get order, not HTTP 1): mappings refer to activities by name, and renaming one updates them.
Give every API branch a reply, including the error branches.

6. The activity tabs

InputThe mapper: values that come from earlier activities (see Mapping data).
OutputThe fields this activity produces, before any run; after a run, the values it received and produced.
SettingsRetries with a growing delay, a timeout, a breakpoint for debugging, and skip this activity.

SettingWhat it doesDefault

7. Mapping data

Select an activity and open Input. Sutra Data on the left lists everything the activity can use: $_projectVariables, $_sengineVariables (read only), $_sutraContext (this run: id, name, version, step), $_sutraVariables, the previous step as input, and every earlier activity by name. Activity Input on the right lists what the activity needs; for structured inputs, the tree of the chosen schema.

Procedure

  1. Drag a field from the left onto a target field on the right. A line shows the link.
  2. Or select a target and write its formula in the box below. Click a function in the library to insert it; the preview under the box shows the result against the last test run.
  3. Drop a list onto a repeating target: a For-Each is created and fields with the same names are mapped. Inside it, {item.x} is the current row and {index} its position.
  4. Click Auto map to map every field that has the same name on both sides.
  5. Click any field, on either side, to highlight where it is mapped; other lines fade.

For-Each, If and Choose

  • Where keeps only rows where a condition holds, using the row's own column names: upper-case(Country) = 'INDIA'.
  • Group by makes one element per distinct value; inside, {group.key}, {group.items} and {group.count}.
  • Sort by orders the rows, ascending or descending.
  • If includes the target only when its condition is true.
  • Choose takes the first When whose condition is true, otherwise the Otherwise value.

Formulas

A formula starts with = in a plain field, and is implied in mapping targets. References are written in braces: {input.name}, {nodes.Get order.body.id}, {gv.OUTBOX}, {vars.total}.

=concat('Name : ', {input.name})
=upper-case(substring-before({input.email}, '@'))
=format-date('DD-MM-YY', {nodes.Parse XML.Order.date})
=format-dateTime('DD MMM YYYY HH:mm', current-dateTime(), 'Asia/Kolkata')
=string-to-base64(concat({gv.USER}, ':', {gv.PASSWORD}))
=if({input.amount} > 1000, 'bulk', 'retail')
={input.rows}[upper-case(Country) = 'INDIA']        rows where the condition holds
=count({input.rows}[Amount > 1000])
={input.rows}[1].City                                  first row, then a field
=xs:integer({input.qty})
=concat({gv.OUT}, '\', current-timestamp('YYYYMMDD'), '.csv')
=set-project-variable('LAST_RUN', current-dateTime())

Backslashes in quoted text are literal, so Windows paths need no escaping. Write a quote twice to include it: 'O''Brien'. Function names ignore case. Every function is listed in Function reference.

Templates in text fields

Text fields such as an email body or a log message use {{ }} templates with pipes: Order {{input.id | upper}} for {{input.amount | number:2}}. The pipes are listed in Template pipes.

When to use JSONata instead

For heavy reshaping of repeating JSON (filter, group, total and nest in one go) a single [[jsonata

activity is often clearer than many mapper rules.]]

8. Schemas and WSDLs

Activities that receive or produce structured data let you pick a shared schema: Manual start (payload), REST service (request body), Send HTTP request (body and response), Map data (target), Parse/Render JSON and XML, the file activities (CSV row schema), Invoke SOAP service (arguments and response).

  • With a schema, later activities see the fields in the mapper before any run, with types and repeating markers.
  • Without one, SutraFlow infers the fields from the test data or the first run.
  • Activities keep their standard fields when a schema is chosen: for example Read file still returns the file name, path and size next to the rows, and Write file always returns the written file's details.

An XSD with several global elements is chosen as Schema::Element. A WSDL added under Service descriptors appears in Invoke SOAP service, which lists its services, ports and operations.

9. Variables and the deployment config

KindRead asSet whereLifetime
Sutra variables{vars.name}Sutra properties; Set variablesOne run.
Project variables{gv.NAME}, {{gv.NAME}}, get-project-variable('NAME')Project → Configuration; the deployment config; set-project-variableKept; a value set at run time lasts until the server restarts or the config changes.
Sengine variables{ev.NAME}, {{ev.NAME}}, get-sengine-variable('NAME')Server & APIs (administrator)Kept; shared by every project on the server. Sutras read them only.

Project variables have a type: string, number, boolean or secret. A secret variable holds the name of a vault secret, never the value.

Read Sengine variables, do not change them

Sengine variables are mostly engine settings (a region, a data centre, a shared folder) that every project relies on. Read them in Sutras; change them only in Server & APIs. set-sengine-variable works only when the administrator ticks Allow Sutras to change Sengine variables, and one Sutra could then change the behaviour of every project.

The deployment config file

Operations staff change settings per environment without opening the studio. The deployment config holds overrides for project variables, resource settings (hosts, ports, URLs, queue names) and logging. Export it from the project, edit it, and import it, or place it at data/config/<project>.json.

{
  "variables": { "OUTBOX": "D:\\exports", "API_BASE": "${env:ORDERS_API:-https://test.example.com}" },
  "resources": { "Orders DB": { "host": "${env:DB_HOST}", "port": 5432 } },
  "logging":   { "path": "D:\\logs\\orders.log", "level": "info" }
}

${env:NAME} reads an environment variable of the server; ${env:NAME:-default} gives a default.

Logging

Each project writes its own log file: path, level, text or JSON lines, rotation by size, and optionally each step's input and output. Set it under Configuration or in the deployment config.

10. Testing and debugging

Test runs the draft once with the trigger's test data. Each activity shows a status dot; select one and open Output to read what it received and produced. API triggers use their test request, message and file triggers their test message or event.

Debug runs the draft one activity at a time:

  1. Optionally set breakpoints: Settings tab → Breakpoint: pause here when debugging.
  2. Click Debug. The run pauses before the first activity. The canvas outlines it, and its Output tab shows the input it will receive.
  3. Step runs that activity and pauses before the next. Continue runs to the next breakpoint. Pause stops before the next activity. Stop cancels the run.

Runs

The Runs screen lists every run: Sutra, version, trigger, status, time. Open one to see each step with its input, output, time and error, and the run log. Approvals lists runs waiting for a person.

11. Deploying and versions

The Sutra you edit is a draft. Deploy saves it as the next version (v1, v2, ...) and makes it live: its timer, file, email, message or Drive trigger starts listening, and its REST or SOAP service is published on the gateway.

  • Runs already in progress finish on the version they started with.
  • Editing after a deploy changes only the draft until you deploy again.
  • Other systems start a deployed Sutra with the Run API: POST /api/flows/{flowId}/run?wait=30000 with { "input": { ... } }.

12. Exposing APIs: security and TLS

A REST service or SOAP service trigger publishes the Sutra on the gateway. Server & APIs lists every exposed service with its addresses and security policy.

API security policy

Create a policy in Resources → API security policy and pick it on the trigger. It checks, in order: HTTPS required, IP allow list (addresses or IPv4 ranges), caller authentication, then a rate limit per caller. CORS origins are optional.

AuthenticationHow callers prove who they are
NoneOpen to anyone. For testing only.
BasicUser name and password; passwords are vault secrets.
API keyA key in a header; keys are vault secrets.
JWT bearerA signed token, checked with a JWKS URL, a public key or a shared secret; issuer, audience and scopes.
WS-Security UsernameTokenSOAP only; password digest with a time window and replay protection.
Mutual TLSA client certificate signed by the client CA set in Server & APIs; optionally only listed subjects.

TLS certificate of the gateway

  • Self-signed: for testing.
  • Own certificate: paste the PEM chain and key; the key is checked against the certificate and stored encrypted.
  • Let's Encrypt: enter the domains and an email. The gateway's HTTP port must be reachable as port 80 on each domain. Start with staging; certificates renew 30 days before they expire, without dropping connections.
  • Client CA: enables mutual TLS for policies that use it.

TLS 1.2 is the minimum.

13. Calling services: REST, SOAP and WS-Security

Outbound calls take two shared resources:

  • HTTP connection: base URL, timeout, default headers, certificate checking, extra trusted CAs, client certificate and key for mutual TLS, proxy.
  • Outbound security: how SutraFlow proves who it is.

Circuit breaker

When a service is down, waiting for every call to time out slows every run. On the HTTP connection, set Open the circuit after to a number of failures in a row (errors or 5xx replies). The circuit then opens: calls through that connection fail at once with "Circuit open" for the time you set, then one trial call decides whether it closes again. SOAP faults do not count; they mean the service is up. Combine it with retries and an error output that, for example, queues the work for later.

MethodForWhat is sent
BasicREST, SOAPAuthorization: Basic
BearerREST, SOAPAuthorization: Bearer
API keyREST, SOAPA header or query parameter.
OAuth 2.0 client credentialsREST, SOAPA token from the token URL, cached until it expires.
Custom headersREST, SOAPAny headers; values may use {{secret.X}}.
WS-Security UsernameTokenSOAPPassword digest (nonce and created) or text, optional timestamp.
WS-Security SAML tokenSOAPA SAML 1.1 or 2.0 assertion from the vault or from an earlier step (for example a token service call).
WS-Security X.509SOAPA binary security token and an XML signature over Body and Timestamp.

See Send HTTP request and Invoke SOAP service.

14. Messaging: Kafka, RabbitMQ and ActiveMQ

The Service Bus palette works the JMS way: Publish message sends, Message subscriber starts a run per message, and Confirm message acknowledges at a point you choose.

  • Put queue and topic names in project variables ({{gv.ORDER_QUEUE}}) so each environment can use its own.
  • JMS headers: delivery mode (persistent or not), priority, time to live, message id, correlation id, reply-to and type; plus your own properties.
  • Acknowledgement: auto on receipt, client after the run succeeds, explicit with Confirm message. On failure: requeue, or send to the dead-letter queue after a number of redeliveries.

15. Files

File activities read and write text, CSV rows, lines, JSON, XML and binary (base64) in UTF-8, UTF-16, ISO-8859-1, Windows-1252 and other encodings.

  • With a row schema, CSV and lines become typed, repeating rows, ready for a For-Each in the mapper.
  • List / read directory takes wildcards: C:\in\*.csv, or =concat({gv.DIR}, '\*.csv').
  • Write file appends or overwrites, and always returns the file's name, path, size and what it did.
  • File trigger reacts to added, modified and removed files; move processed files away with Move / copy / delete file.

16. Databases, email, Firebase and apps

  • DB Ops works with PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite. Parameters are written :name and are always bound, never pasted into the SQL.
  • Email: SMTP to send, IMAP to start a run per incoming message.
  • Firebase: Firestore, Realtime Database and push notifications, with a service-account key held in the vault.
  • Apps (Google Sheets, Drive and Docs, Dropbox, YouTube, Facebook Pages) use an OAuth connection: create it in Resources, then click Connect account and sign in once. Tokens are stored in the vault and refreshed automatically. Connected API call reaches any other API of the same account.

17. Custom code, HTML and AI

  • JavaScript code runs your JavaScript in a sandbox without host access, with time and memory limits.
  • HTML template builds HTML with escaped placeholders, loops and conditions.
  • Transform (JSONata) transforms JSON with one expression.
  • The AI palette: AI prompt, AI classify, AI router, AI extract, AI summarize, AI translate and AI sentiment. Each also returns ai: the provider, engine, model, input, output and total tokens, and the time taken.

AI providers

An AI provider connection chooses the engine. Several can exist side by side, for example a fast one for routing and a strong one for summaries.

EngineWhat it needsDefault model
Claude APIAn Anthropic API key in the vault.claude-opus-5-5; also claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5
Gemini APIA Google AI Studio or Vertex API key.gemini-3-pro-preview; also other Gemini 3 models
OpenAI APIAn OpenAI API key. Any compatible server works with its own API base URL.gpt-5
OllamaAn Ollama server; on this machine by default (http://127.0.0.1:11434). A full endpoint such as http://localhost:11434/api/generate also works, and the Ollama API setting chooses chat or generate. No key; nothing leaves your network, so it works offline.The first model installed, or the one you pick
LM StudioLM Studio's local server (http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1).The model loaded in LM Studio
Hugging FaceA Hugging Face token; uses Hugging Face Inference Providers.A model id such as Qwen/Qwen3-8B
Hugging Face TGI (local)Text Generation Inference running on your machine (default http://127.0.0.1:8090/v1; SutraFlow's gateway uses 8080).The model TGI serves
OpenAI-compatible serverAny server with the OpenAI chat API: llama.cpp, vLLM, LocalAI, Jan. Key only when the server asks for one.The server's first model, or the one you pick
Claude CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenAI Codex CLIThe command-line tool installed and signed in on the server (claude, gemini, codex). Uses that tool's own account.The tool's default, or the one you set

Click List models to see the models the engine offers and pick one; Test connection shows which model answered, with tokens and time.

Adding models to Ollama, online or offline

  • Pull a model by name, such as qwen3, when the Ollama machine has internet.
  • Import from a path on this server when it does not. Copy the files over (USB drive, share), then give their path: a .gguf file; a Modelfile (FROM file.gguf, with TEMPLATE, SYSTEM and PARAMETER); a Safetensors model folder; or an Ollama models folder copied from another machine (it holds manifests and blobs), with the model to take from it. SutraFlow sends the files to Ollama through its API and registers them under the name you choose.

One setting per environment

The deployment config overrides any connection setting, the engine included. Test with a local Ollama and run production on another engine without changing a Sutra:

"resources": { "AI provider": { "engine": "Claude API", "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "apiKeySecret": "ANTHROPIC_KEY" } }
Command-line tools

The prompt is sent to the tool on standard input, never on the command line, and the tool runs in an empty folder as the SutraFlow server user. Keep the tool's own permissions for running commands and editing files switched off: a message from outside could otherwise ask it to act on the server.

Guidelines

Route AI decisions that matter (money, customers) through [[approval

until you trust them.]]

18. AI skills over MCP

A Sutra that starts with an MCP skill trigger is a skill: AI assistants such as Claude connect to SutraFlow over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), see the skills, and call them. Each call runs the Sutra with the arguments the AI chose, and Reply to AI sends the outcome back. Skills can do anything a Sutra does: write a CSV file, post to a Facebook page, look up an order in a database, start an approval.

Build a skill

  1. Under Resources, add an MCP server: its address on the gateway (for example /mcp/orders), a title, instructions for the AI, and an API security policy. One server holds many skills.
  2. Create a Sutra that starts with MCP skill, choose the server, and describe the tool: name, title, what it does and when to use it, and its inputs.
  3. Build the work, and end every branch with Reply to AI; on error branches tick Is an error.
  4. Test it in the studio with the trigger's test arguments, then Deploy. Server & APIs lists each skill with its address.

Connect an assistant

Give the assistant the server's address and, when a policy is set, the key or token as a header. With Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http orders https://your-server:8443/mcp/orders --header "X-API-Key: your-key"

Other assistants that support MCP over HTTP take the same address and header. Skills without a server are at /mcp.

Sample skills

Add sample Sutras also adds an MCP server named Sample skills (/mcp/samples) with two skills: Skill: Write CSV file and Skill: Post to Facebook page. Choose a security policy on the server, a Facebook connection and page on the second skill, and deploy them.

Guidelines

Protect every MCP server with an API security policy: a skill acts with the server's rights.
Tick Changes data on skills that create, change or delete something, so the assistant asks the user first.
Write descriptions for someone who has never seen the Sutra: the AI chooses skills by them.

19. Secrets and studio security

  • Passwords, keys and tokens live in the vault (Resources → Secrets), encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Settings hold the secret's name.
  • Secret values are never returned by the API. A secret used in a step is masked in stored outputs and logs.
  • The studio listens on 127.0.0.1 by default. Sessions are HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookies; every change needs a request header that browsers cannot forge across sites; repeated failed sign-ins are slowed down.

20. Running in production

  1. Set SUTRA_MASTER_KEY from your secret store, or protect and back up data/master.key.
  2. Keep the studio on 127.0.0.1, or behind a VPN.
  3. Set the gateway certificate (own or Let's Encrypt) and require HTTPS in every API policy.
  4. Put environment-specific values in the deployment config, with ${env:NAME} for anything secret or host-specific.
  5. Set each project's log file and level; rotate by size.
  6. Back up the data folder regularly.

21. Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and remedy
A mapping shows not runThe activity was on a branch that was not taken in the last test. Test with data that takes that branch.
An API caller waits a minute, then gets 504A branch ended without Send HTTP response or SOAP reply. Add replies on every branch, including error branches.
A timer or file trigger does nothingOnly the deployed version listens. Deploy, then check the listeners table in Server & APIs.
Required fields not mappedThe Input tab names them. Map them, or remove the requirement from the schema.
Formula errorThe preview under the formula names the problem: an unknown function, a missing bracket, or a quote not doubled.
The run stops after 10000 stepsA loop that never ends. Check the condition that leaves it.
Let's Encrypt failsPort 80 on the domain must reach the gateway's HTTP port.

22. Activity reference

Triggers

▶Manual start

Palettes → Triggers · activity type start · trigger

Starts the Sutra from the studio or the Run API, with a test payload.

In scope

  • A test payload in JSON, and an optional payload schema that describes it for mapping.
Out of scope
  • Starting on a schedule, a request, a file or a message: use the trigger made for it.

When to use it

  • A process that another process or system starts on demand.
  • Building and testing a process before you choose its real trigger.

When to choose another activity

  • Run on a schedule → use Timer.
  • Expose the process as a REST API → use REST service.

Procedure

  1. Drag Manual start onto an empty canvas (a new flow already has one).
  2. In the General tab, write a test payload in JSON.
  3. Optionally pick a payload schema, so later steps see its fields in the mapper.

Output

  • The payload: either what the Run API sent, or the test payload.

⏱Timer

Palettes → Triggers · activity type timer · trigger

Starts the Sutra on a schedule while the Sutra is deployed: a cron expression or a fixed interval.

In scope
  • Cron expressions with optional seconds and a time zone.
  • A fixed interval in seconds.
  • A fixed payload added to every run, plus firedAt.
Out of scope
  • Missed runs while the server was stopped are not run afterwards.
  • Calendars of holidays: test the date in an If / else after the timer.

When to use it

  • Nightly exports, polling an API every few minutes, a daily report.

When to choose another activity

  • React to new files instead of polling → use File trigger.
  • React to queue messages → use Message subscriber.

Procedure

  1. Choose cron or interval.
  2. For cron, write the expression, for example 0 30 9 * * MON-FRI, and the time zone.
  3. Deploy the Sutra. The timer runs only while the deployed version is active.

Output

  • The payload fields and firedAt (ISO date and time).
Guidelines
  • Put the schedule in a project variable ({{gv.EXPORT_CRON}}) so operations can change it per environment.

⇲REST service

Palettes → Triggers · activity type restService · trigger

Exposes the Sutra as an HTTP/REST API on the gateway. Reply with a Send HTTP response step.

In scope
  • One HTTP method and path per trigger, with :name path parameters.
  • An API security policy: Basic, API key, JWT, mutual TLS, IP allow list, rate limit, CORS.
  • JSON, XML, form and text bodies; a body schema for mapping.
Out of scope
  • Several paths in one trigger: use one REST service per path, or a path parameter.
  • Validation of the body against the schema (use Validate fields).

When to use it

  • Publishing a Sutra as an API for partners, apps and other systems.

When to choose another activity

  • Publish a SOAP web service with a WSDL → use SOAP service.
  • Receive work from a queue instead of HTTP → use Message subscriber.

Procedure

  1. Choose the method and the path, for example GET /orders/:id.
  2. Pick an API security policy (Resources → API security policy).
  3. Write a test request so you can test without a caller.
  4. End each branch with Send HTTP response.
  5. Deploy. The API is served by the gateway on ports 8080 and 8443.

Output

  • method, path, params, query, headers, body, auth (the caller after the policy check) and client (IP address, HTTPS).
Guidelines
  • Never deploy without a policy outside testing.
  • Always reply on the error branch too, or the caller waits until the reply timeout (60 seconds by default).

⧉SOAP service

Palettes → Triggers · activity type soapService · trigger

Exposes the Sutra as a SOAP web service with a generated WSDL. Each operation is an output; reply with a SOAP reply step.

In scope
  • A SOAP 1.1 or 1.2 service with a generated WSDL at ?wsdl.

  • The same API security policies as REST, plus WS-Security UsernameToken.
Out of scope
  • Importing an existing WSDL to define the service contract.
  • WS-Security encryption of incoming messages.

When to use it

  • Replacing or fronting a SOAP service that partners already call.

When to choose another activity

  • Publish JSON over HTTP → use REST service.
  • Call someone else's SOAP service → use Invoke SOAP service.

Procedure

  1. Name the service and namespace, and the path (for example /soap/orders).
  2. List the operations, separated by commas. Each becomes an output port.
  3. Connect each operation to its steps and end each with SOAP reply.
  4. Deploy, then give callers https://host:8443/soap/orders?wsdl.

Output

  • operation, body (the operation element as data), header, soapAction, auth, client.

✧MCP skill

Palettes → Triggers · activity type mcpTool · trigger

Makes the Sutra a tool (skill) that AI assistants such as Claude can call over the Model Context Protocol, at the gateway address /mcp. Describe what it does and what it needs; end the Sutra with Reply to AI.

In scope
  • Making a Sutra a skill (tool) that AI assistants such as Claude call over the Model Context Protocol.
  • A name, a title and a description the AI reads; inputs as rows or a JSON schema; an optional result schema.
  • An MCP server to group skills under one address, and an API security policy.
Out of scope
  • Calling other MCP servers from a Sutra.
  • Streaming partial results.

When to use it

  • Letting an assistant do real work through your Sutras: write a CSV file, post to a Facebook page, look up an order, raise a ticket.

When to choose another activity

  • Expose the Sutra to programs instead of AI assistants → use REST service.

Procedure

  1. Create an MCP server under Resources (address such as /mcp/orders, instructions, security policy), or leave the server empty to use /mcp.
  2. Drag MCP skill onto a new Sutra and choose the server.
  3. Give a tool name and a description that says what it does, when to use it and what it returns.
  4. List the inputs: one row each, with a description; start it with number:, array: and so on for other types, and optional: when it may be left out.
  5. Tick Changes data when it creates, changes or deletes something.
  6. End every branch with Reply to AI, and Deploy.

Output

  • arguments (what the AI sent), tool, auth (the caller after the policy check) and client.
Guidelines
  • The description is what the AI chooses by: write it for a person who has never seen the Sutra.
  • A skill that changes data should be confirmed by the user; assistants do so when Changes data is ticked.

■End

Palettes → Flow control · activity type end

Ends a branch and records its result. Can also stop the whole Sutra at once, as succeeded or failed, cancelling the other branches.

In scope
  • Ending a branch and recording its result.
  • Stopping the whole Sutra at once, as succeeded or failed: other branches still running or waiting are cancelled.
Out of scope
  • Replying to an API caller: use Send HTTP response or SOAP reply first.

When to use it

  • this branch: the normal end of a path.
  • Sutra: success: the work is done and nothing else should run, for example after a duplicate is detected.
  • Sutra: error: stop everything and mark the run failed, for example on an error output when no recovery is possible.

When to choose another activity

  • Fail a branch so an error handler can catch it → use Throw error.

Procedure

  1. Choose what ends: this branch, Sutra: success or Sutra: error.
  2. For Sutra: error, write the error message; it appears as the run's error in Runs and in the log.
  3. Connect it after the last step, or to an error output.

Output

  • The result, recorded as the run's output.

⤷Call Sutra

Palettes → Flow control · activity type callProcess

Runs another Sutra of this project with the input you give it and, when Wait is on, continues with its result (set by its Return activity). Build a piece of logic once and call it from many Sutras.

In scope
  • Running another Sutra of the same project with an input you set or map, and continuing with its result.
  • Waiting for the result, or starting it and continuing at once.
  • The draft while testing, the deployed version when deployed.
Out of scope
  • Sutras of other projects.
  • More than 10 levels of Sutras calling Sutras.

When to use it

  • Logic used by several Sutras: customer lookup, address cleaning, sending a standard alert.
  • Breaking a large Sutra into readable parts.

When to choose another activity

  • Signal other processes without waiting → use Send to channel.

Procedure

  1. Build the called Sutra: a Manual start (with a payload schema) and a Return at the end.
  2. In the calling Sutra, add Call Sutra and choose the Sutra.
  3. Set the input as a value, or choose mapping and map it to the payload schema in the Input tab.
  4. Optionally pick a result schema, so later steps see the result's fields.
  5. Connect the error output: a failure inside the called Sutra arrives there.

Output

  • With Wait on: the called Sutra's Return result. With Wait off: runId, process, started.
Guidelines
  • A called run appears in Runs as its own run with source sutra.
  • Deploy the called Sutra before the calling one, or deployed calls fail with "not deployed".

Outputs (ports)

out error

⚠Error handler

Palettes → Flow control · activity type catch

Runs when any activity fails and its own error output is not connected. Other branches stop; the handler's path decides how the run ends (End with process: error to mark it failed). One per process.

In scope
  • One error handler per Sutra, started by the engine when an activity fails and its own error output is not connected.
  • The error (message, activity name and type, time) and the failed activity's input.
Out of scope
  • Errors already handled by a connected error output.
  • Errors inside the handler's own path: those fail the run.

When to use it

  • A common way to log, alert and clean up for every activity of a Sutra, instead of wiring each error output.

When to choose another activity

  • Handle one activity's error differently → use Throw error.

Procedure

  1. Drag Error handler onto the canvas. It has no input connection.
  2. Connect its output to the steps to run on an error, for example Log and Send email.
  3. End the path with End: Sutra: error marks the run failed; otherwise the run counts as handled and ends as done.

Output

  • error (message, step, type, at) and input, the failed activity's input.
Guidelines
  • When the handler starts, the Sutra's other branches stop.

Outputs (ports)

out

Also has the Settings tab every activity shares: retries, timeout, skip and breakpoint.

Files

🗀File trigger

Palettes → Files · activity type fileTrigger · trigger

Starts the Sutra when a file in a folder is added, modified or removed (polling while the Sutra is deployed). Can read the file as text or as structured rows.

In scope
  • A folder with a wildcard pattern (*.csv, orders-*.xml), optionally with sub-folders.
  • Added, modified and removed events, each its own output.
  • Reading the file: text, CSV rows or lines typed by a schema, JSON, XML or base64, in the chosen encoding.
Out of scope
  • Remote folders (FTP, SFTP).

When to use it

  • Processing files dropped by another system or by people.

When to choose another activity

  • Sutra every file already in a folder → use List / read directory.

Procedure

  1. Enter the folder, for example {{gv.INBOX}}, and the pattern.
  2. Tick the events you need; each becomes an output.
  3. Set stable for seconds so files still being copied are not read early.
  4. Choose how to read the content. For CSV, pick a row schema to get typed, repeating rows.
  5. Move or delete the file at the end with Move / copy / delete file, so it is not picked up again after a restart.

Output

  • event and the file details (name, path, relativePath, folder, extension, size, modifiedAt), plus the content fields of the chosen format.

Outputs (ports)

added modified removed

⇩Message subscriber

Palettes → Service Bus · activity type busSubscribe · trigger

Starts the Sutra for each message on a queue or topic while deployed. Gives the body, the JMS headers and the custom properties. Acknowledge automatically, after the Sutra succeeds, or with a Confirm message activity.

In scope
  • Queues and topics, selectors, durable subscriptions, Kafka consumer groups.
  • Acknowledgement: auto (on receipt), client (after the run succeeds) or explicit (Confirm message).
  • On failure: requeue, or dead-letter after a number of redeliveries; concurrency.
Out of scope
  • Exactly-once processing: design steps so a message processed twice does no harm.

When to use it

  • Processing work from a queue, reacting to events.

Procedure

  1. Choose the broker, connection and destination.
  2. Choose the acknowledgement mode; client suits most Sutras.
  3. Choose what happens on failure and how many messages run at once.
  4. Write a test message so you can test without a broker.
  5. Deploy; the subscriber runs while the deployed version is active.

Output

  • body, headers (JMS headers), properties, destination, redelivered.

out

24. Function reference

123 functions for formulas and mappings, grouped as in the mapper's function library. Names ignore case.

String

FunctionWhat it doesExample
concat(a, b, ...)Joins text values.concat('Name : ', {input.name})
substring(text, start, length?)Part of the text; start counts from 1.substring('ABCDEF', 2, 3) = 'BCD'
substring-before(text, find)Text before the first match.substring-before('a@b.com', '@') = 'a'
substring-after(text, find)Text after the first match.substring-after('a@b.com', '@') = 'b.com'
substring-before-last(text, find)Text before the last match.
substring-after-last(text, find)Text after the last match.substring-after-last('a/b/c.txt', '/') = 'c.txt'
upper-case(text)Upper case.
lower-case(text)Lower case.
trim(text)Removes spaces at both ends.
left-trim(text)Removes leading spaces.
right-trim(text)Removes trailing spaces.
normalize-space(text)Trims and collapses inner spaces.
string-length(text)Number of characters.
contains(text, find)True when text contains find.
starts-with(text, prefix)True when text starts with prefix.
ends-with(text, suffix)True when text ends with suffix.
index-of(text, find)Position of find (1-based), 0 when absent.
replace(text, find, with)Replaces every occurrence (plain text).
replace-regex(text, pattern, with)Regular expression replace; $1 refers to groups.
matches(text, pattern)True when the regular expression matches.
translate(text, from, to)Replaces characters one for one.
pad(text, length, char?)Pads on the right.
pad-front(text, length, char?)Pads on the left, e.g. leading zeros.pad-front(42, 6, '0') = '000042'
tokenize(text, separator)Splits text into a list.
string-join(list, separator)Joins a list into text.
capitalize(text)First letter of each word upper case.

Conversion

FunctionWhat it doesExample
xs:string(value)Converts to text (objects become JSON).
xs:integer(value)Whole number (fraction dropped); error when not a number.
xs:int(value)Same as xs:integer.
xs:long(value)Same as xs:integer.
xs:decimal(value)Decimal number; error when not a number.
xs:double(value)Floating-point number (NaN when not a number).
xs:float(value)Same as xs:double.
xs:date(value)Date as YYYY-MM-DD.
xs:dateTime(value)Date and time as ISO 8601.
xs:time(value)Time as HH:mm:ss.
xs:boolean(value)Converts to true/false ("true", "1" and "yes" are true).

Encode/Decode

FunctionWhat it doesExample
string-to-base64(text)Base64 encode.
base64-to-string(base64)Base64 decode.
url-encode(text)Encode for URLs.
url-decode(text)Decode URL encoding.
hex-encode(text)Text to hexadecimal.
hex-decode(hex)Hexadecimal to text.
escape-xml(text)Escape < > & ' " for XML.
unescape-xml(text)Undo XML escaping.
md5(text)MD5 hash (hex).
sha1(text)SHA-1 hash (hex).
sha256(text)SHA-256 hash (hex).
hmac-sha256(key, text, encoding?)HMAC signature, hex or base64.
to-json(value)Data to JSON text.
from-json(text)JSON text to data.

Variables

FunctionWhat it doesExample
get-project-variable('NAME')Current value of a project variable (same as {gv.NAME}, but the name can be computed).
set-project-variable('NAME', value)Changes a project variable for every later run (kept until the next deployment config change). Returns the value.
get-sengine-variable('NAME')Sengine variable: a server setting made by the administrator in Server & APIs, shared by all projects. Read it; do not change it from Sutras.
set-sengine-variable('NAME', value)Changes a Sengine variable for every project. Not advised: works only when the administrator allows it in Server & APIs.

Utility

FunctionWhat it doesExample
newline()A line break, for concat().
tab()A tab character.
uuid()A new random id (UUID v4).
timestamp(date?)Milliseconds since 1970 (now when empty).timestamp() = 1791900000000
timestamp-seconds(date?)Seconds since 1970 (Unix time).
current-timestamp(format?, timezone?)Now as text; default 'YYYYMMDDHHmmssSSS', handy for file names and ids.concat('orders-', current-timestamp('YYYYMMDD-HHmmss'), '.csv')
random-string(length, characters?)Random letters and digits.
type-of(value)text, number, boolean, list, object or null.
hostname()Name of the server running the Sutra.
file-name(path)Last part of a path: C:\in\a.csv gives a.csv.
file-base-name(path)File name without its extension.
file-extension(path)Extension without the dot (csv).
dir-name(path)Folder part of a path.
path-join(a, b, ...)Joins path parts with one separator.path-join({gv.INBOX}, '*.csv')
format-bytes(bytes)Human size: 1536 gives 1.5 KB.
default(value, fallback)The value, or fallback when it is empty.
json-path(object, path)Reads a nested field by path text: json-path({input}, 'order.lines[0].sku').

Date/Time

FunctionWhat it doesExample
current-dateTime()Now, ISO 8601 (UTC).
current-date()Today as YYYY-MM-DD (server time zone).
current-time()Time now as HH:mm:ss.
format-date(format, date, timezone?)Formats a date. Tokens: YYYY YY MMMM MMM MM DD dddd ddd; text in [brackets] stays.format-date('DD-MM-YY', {input.date})
format-time(format, date, timezone?)Formats a time. Tokens: HH hh mm ss SSS A Z.format-time('hh:mm A', {input.at})
format-dateTime(format, date, timezone?)Formats date and time, e.g. in Asia/Kolkata.format-dateTime('DD MMM YYYY HH:mm', {now}, 'Asia/Kolkata')
parse-date(format, text)Reads a date written in the given format; returns ISO 8601.parse-date('DD/MM/YYYY', '31/12/2026')
add-to-date(date, years, months, days)Adds (or with negatives subtracts) years, months and days.
add-to-dateTime(date, years, months, days, hours, minutes, seconds)Adds to a date-time.
days-between(from, to)Whole days from one date to another.
year-from-date(date)Year number.
month-from-date(date)Month number 1 to 12.
day-from-date(date)Day of month.
from-timestamp(ms)Milliseconds since 1970 to ISO date.

Number

FunctionWhat it doesExample
number(value)Converts to a number (commas and currency signs removed).
round(number, decimals?)Rounds half up.
floor(number)Rounds down.
ceiling(number)Rounds up.
abs(number)Absolute value.
power(base, exponent)Base to the power.
format-number(number, pattern)Formats with a pattern such as '#,##0.00'.format-number(1234.5, '#,##0.00') = '1,234.50'
sum(list, field?)Total of a list, or of a field in each item.
avg(list, field?)Average.
min(a, b, ...) or min(list)Smallest value.
max(a, b, ...) or max(list)Largest value.
random(min, max)Random whole number between min and max.
is-number(value)True when the value is a number.

Logical

FunctionWhat it doesExample
if(condition, then, else)Chooses a value; only the chosen side is evaluated.if({input.qty} > 10, 'bulk', 'retail')
coalesce(a, b, ...)First value that is not empty.coalesce({input.mobile}, {input.phone}, 'n/a')
not(value)True when the value is false or empty.
equals-ignore-case(a, b)Case-insensitive comparison.

Sequence

FunctionWhat it doesExample
exists(value)True when the field is present (even if empty text).
empty(value)True when missing, empty text or an empty list.
last() or last(list)Inside a For-Each or [filter]: number of items; with a list: its last item.
position()Inside a For-Each or [filter]: position of the current item (from 1).{input.rows}[position() <= 10]
count(list)Number of items (0 when missing, 1 for a single value).
item-at(list, position)Item at a position (1-based).
first(list)First item.
distinct(list)Removes duplicates.

List

FunctionWhat it doesExample
pluck(list, field)Takes one field from every item.
sort(list, field?, descending?)Sorts a list.
filter-by(list, field, value)Items whose field equals value.
list(a, b, ...)Makes a list.
group-by(list, field)Groups items by a field: a list of { key, items, count }.group-by({input.orders}, 'customer')
count-by(list, field)How many items have each value: { value: count }.
flatten(list, childField?)Flattens nested lists; with a child field, one item per child carrying its parent as _parent.flatten({input.orders}, 'lines')
slice(list, start, count?)Part of a list; start counts from 1.
concat-lists(list, list, ...)Joins lists into one.
contains-item(list, value)True when the list holds the value.
object('key', value, 'key2', value2, ...)Builds an object from key/value pairs.
merge(object, object, ...)Combines objects; later fields win.
